summary: A 1974 description of the second version of the procedure call documents, a host-level protocol used in the NSW system. It is a slightly constrained version of the ARPANET host-to-host protocol, with changes affecting allocation, RFNM waiting and retransmission. See also RFC 684.

plainLanguage.summary: One computer asks another to run a task, like calling a helper. This note gives the rules for those calls on an early network system.

subtitle: An announcement of version 2 of the Procedure Call Protocol document set used by the National Software Works.

tldr.problem: SRI's team on the National Software Works (NSW) project needed a protocol for the modules that make up the system to call procedures in one another.
tldr.mechanism: The Procedure Call Protocol (PCP) and a family of companion documents define the call environment, packages of procedures, data formats and a slightly constrained host-level protocol.
tldr.outcome: Version 2 is described as substantially different from Version 1 and obsoletes it and all intermediate informal PCP documents. The authors ask for comments.

today: RFC 674 is a 1974 announcement whose status is listed as Unknown, with no RFC recorded as obsoleting or updating it. The text itself says that Version 2 replaces Version 1 and the informal PCP documents.

sections.title: What Is Being Announced
sections.content:
RFC 674, from Jon Postel and Jim White of SRI-ARC, announces the second published version of several National Software Works (NSW) and Procedure Call Protocol (PCP) documents. SRI is part of a team on the NSW project, and developed PCP for use between the modules that make up the NSW.

Version 2 is described as SUBSTANTIALLY different from Version 1, and it and all intermediate informally distributed PCP documents are obsoleted by this release. Comments are invited. Each document is available online as an NLS file and as a formatted text file reachable by FTP with anonymous login.
sections.plainLanguage: A team building a shared computer workshop is sharing the second edition of its rule books and asking people what they think.

sections.title: The Document Set
sections.content:
The core is PCP itself, which describes the virtual programming environment and the inter-process exchanges that implement it. Three packages run in that setting: PIP, a procedure-call-level interface that includes calling, resuming, interrupting and aborting remote procedures; PSP, which augments PCP largely for data store manipulation; and PMP, for creating, deleting and interconnecting processes and allocating processors.

Low-level details are in PCPFMT (data structure formats), PCPHST and PCPFRK (the IPC implementations between hosts and between Tenex forks). Service packages are EXEC (identification, accounting and usage), FILE, BATCH and LLDBUG (assembly-level debugging). RJE-MODEL, TBH and BOXES cover remote job entry use, tool bearing host requirements and the Black Boxes of the Works Manager.
sections.plainLanguage: There is one main book, a few helper books on how to use it, some books for the plumbing, and some books for particular jobs like files and batch work.

sections.title: The Host-Level Protocol and Reading Order
sections.content:
The HOST document describes the host level protocol used in the NSW. It is a slightly constrained version of the standard ARPANET host to host protocol, and the constraints affect the allocation, RFNM wait and retransmission policies. The announcement says this topic has little impact on the remainder of the NSW protocols.

Readers are urged to begin with the PCP document, which gives the motivation and the substance of the protocol, then PIP, PSP and PMP. PMP is most relevant to a casual reader, while a programmer coding in the PCP environment should read all three. PCPFMT, PCPHST and PCPFRK are of interest only to PCP implementers.
sections.plainLanguage: Start with the main book. The plumbing books are only for the people who build the pipes.
